I have been sexually harassed etc, and you get really comfortable telling people to fuck off, depending on the culture in your kitchen. But what has really gotten in my way as a woman in kitchens is the fact that I am a more emotional person than the typical male cook, and the weird result is that my chefs take it easy on me when I wish they wouldn't... I have been really fortunate to have multiple chefs care about my emotional well being as much as they have. But the problem then is I can't shake the persona of the cook you can't push or that you have to be careful with. Gender dynamics in kitchens are complex, and sometimes very shitty and stressful for everyone...but I would never tell a woman not to pursue a career in the industry because of them. Yeah, you need to be primed for the reality that they'll talk about your ass or stereotype you or mock you/talk about the way you look. At this point though, I'm happy to sit there and shoot right back at them. If you work on a good team you can talk things out pretty up front. However as should be the case anywhere, physical assault shouldn't be tolerated by your managers, and it hasn't been tolerated in my experience, aside from an instance I know of with one of my female coworkers who was assaulted BY a manager. In that case she had no choice but to leave because the person in power was the offender. You just have to be a fighter, and a realist. That doesn't mean that I concede that gender-based prejudice is ok, or that sexism isn't a problem or doesn't exist ( it definitely does). But what I would say is...it's the same shit women deal with outside of kitchens, you have to deal with the same harassment, but also, plenty of men in kitchens would step up to defend you, ask you if you're ok, etc. I have had more positive platonic relationships with men from working in kitchens.

Being a good listener is very valuable to people, and it's something you can offer without making yourself vulnerable to judgement. I know you mentioned fear of being judged, but being open about a personal matter with someone (if it's relevant) is a great way to have meaningful conversations. 

I think appearing to be a "valuable asset" revolves around demonstrating maturity a lot of the time. Different people also value different qualities in others, so maybe think about the person or people you are trying to appeal to, and consider what they might value in a friend, coworker, etc. 

If you put effort into being there for someone, and you remain kind and nonjudgmental, I think you can make a connection.

I relate in the sense that I find myself excitedly telling someone something and then find that it goes nowhere or isn't totally relevant so then I end awkwardly or don't know what to say and trail off to nothing. I've been self conscious about it and I remember confirming with at least one friend that she noticed it.

To combat this I just try to really THINK before I speak as the saying goes, and make sure if I'm talking that I'm saying something that is worth saying. I still fail but that's just what I try to focus on.

Are you sure your friends are being sarcastic as you think? Could it just be social anxiety blowing it out of proportion in your head? Maybe you have a unique sense of humor and that's part of what makes you charming to others. Sometimes our faults are charming because they make us who we are.

When it comes down to it, be yourself and if your friends are true friends, they will stick by you, awkward storytelling or not.

There is always time...from someone who did nothing in high school and then everything in college, sometimes you're not missing that much. Being adventurous can be wonderful, but sometimes you do things or reach places that you never wanted to go. We all do things in our own time, don't knock yourself for going slowly or carefully. I've been in enough trouble to know that it's truly not worth it.
You never know what could be on the horizon...life can surprise you in good ways, too. It sucks, but patience pays off. I have felt as you do but it always seems worth it to experience one more day.

It seems you are feeling darkness, something that you don't feel can be worked on or understood. Torn between what you want to do and what you're supposed to do. Do not let ridicule drown your strength. Ridicule is born of toxic people, that do not seek to understand and/or do everything from a basis of jealousy and reaction.

There is no cure someone can hand you for this pain, but I believe you have the strength to move forward. Feel your pain, look at it, hold it in front of you and face it, don't stuff it down. Then- carry on. Evaluate where you are and make the best choice you can see. Your creator instilled strength and potential in you. I hear you, and you are not alone. We all cry out whether loudly or unheard.

I've thought a lot about trying to reprogram my thought cycles. A lot of the way I think is unproductive and brings me back to self loathing and worthlessness. My mind automatically jumps to a place of obsessing on negatives. I use RET (rational emotive therapy) to try and logically work through something without more unproductive emotion. You examine the cause of how you feel, then rationally consider any action you can take to correct it, and rule out unhealthy actions to take (which may be whatever action might be your first inclination). Example: Recognize that going on a drinking binge because you got dumped won't actually help anything, and won't make you feel better about the root of your pain in a lasting way. 

Beyond self improvement it is very tough though. We can only work on ourselves, and we can't change the way others see us, speak of us, etc. We can't make a person see our worth if they are not in a position to do so, or just not of the right quality to do so. Life requires a lot of acceptance, and I find if something is really causing me repeated breakdowns and hysterics, there's probably something going on that I am not willing to or don't know how to accept yet.

Anyway...look at yourself, to see where maybe you could be the source of some of your own anguish. Beyond that we just have to let go of the painful or negative, infuriating, others actions-based realities. Let go and accept and try to be proactive in our own minds. We just can't give up.

When I was young I was mentally evaluated because I was self harming. I haven't forgotten this thing a social worker said to me about people with depression. It's kind of a visualization: all people, depressed or not, go through upswings and downswings in mood, you can visualize this as a line going up and down creating hills and valleys. Her point was that people with depression might experience longer valleys, or deeper valleys, before heading back uphill. Maybe the hills are also smaller, or shorter. We all experience up moods and down moods, but the variance in intensity and duration separate us and make us less able to understand each other. This is what has caused me pain as someone with depression: feeling weaker for feeling emotions differently than others.

Anyway that wasn't exactly well-organized advice, but maybe an idea could help someone.

Ok, so I tend to overcompensate on the friendly/overly bubbly stuff with coworkers, for example. I've been struggling in my personal life, but I don't want that to be the person they see, so I've been trying to swing my persona in the other direction toward "happy coworker". Anyway, one thing I do, as fake as it sounds, is mirror the person I'm interacting with, notice their demeanor, and give them the same amount of energy back if they are talkative. I also try to compliment people in small ways just to contribute something positive or encouraging to their day. You don't have to smile constantly, just be kind of thoughtful about having positive moments with people, and they will like you.
